definition:
The canon of Scripture is the collection of books the church receives as the written word of God, and the doctrine of Scripture asks what those books are for the church: where their authority comes from, whether they are enough, whether they can be understood, and whether the church could do without them. The word canon comes from the Greek kanōn, a straight rod used to measure, and from there any ‘rule’ or ‘standard’. Paul uses it for a measure of boundaries (2 Corinthians 10:13) and for a rule to live by, blessing “all who walk by this rule” (Galatians 6:16). The Hebrew qaneh, ‘reed’, gives the same picture of a measuring reed (Ezekiel 40:3). By the fourth century Christians used the word for the list of books, so that canon now carries two senses at once: the list, and the rule by which the church's faith and life are measured. Protestant theology later compressed the second sense into a Latin phrase describing Scripture as the norm that norms every other norm and is not itself normed by any.

The Bible's own vocabulary for itself is plain. The Hebrew sefer means ‘scroll’ or ‘book’, and torah means ‘instruction’, the name first of the five books of Moses and then of God's teaching generally. The New Testament speaks of graphē, ‘writing’, and hai graphai, ‘the Scriptures’; of ta hiera grammata, ‘the sacred writings’ (2 Timothy 3:15); and of ‘the Law and the Prophets’ as a shorthand for the whole. Jewish tradition came to call its Bible the Tanakh, an acronym of its three parts: Torah (Law), Nevi'im (Prophets), and Ketuvim (Writings). The later Protestant theologians gathered the Bible's claims about itself under four headings that this study follows: its authority (it speaks with God's own voice), its necessity (the church cannot know the way of salvation without it), its sufficiency (it gives everything needed for salvation and a godly life), and its clarity (what is necessary can be understood by ordinary readers using ordinary means). How the Bible came to be breathed out by God is treated in the study on revelation; this study asks which books, and what they are for.
ot:
The canon begins where Israel's covenant begins, with a written document. At Sinai the covenant was written down, and when Moses finished writing ‘the words of this law’ he commanded the Levites, “Take this Book of the Law and place it beside the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God, so that it may remain there as a witness against you” (Deuteronomy 31:26). Ancient Near Eastern treaties were deposited in temples in much the same way, and Meredith Kline argued in The Structure of Biblical Authority (1972) that the idea of a canon grows out of this covenant form: a treaty text is by nature fixed and binding. From the start the words were guarded. “You must not add to or subtract from what I command you” (Deuteronomy 4:2), and Proverbs repeats the warning: “Do not add to His words, lest He rebuke you and prove you a liar” (Proverbs 30:6). The book grew under the same authority. Joshua “recorded these things in the Book of the Law of God” (Joshua 24:26), and Samuel wrote the rights of kingship “on a scroll and laid it up before the LORD” (1 Samuel 10:25).

The prophets added a second body of written word, and Israel slowly learned to treat it as Scripture too. Isaiah was told to “Bind up the testimony and seal the law among my disciples” (Isaiah 8:16), and he made the written word the test of every rival voice: “To the law and to the testimony! If they do not speak according to this word, they have no light of dawn” (Isaiah 8:20). When King Jehoiakim burned Jeremiah's scroll around 604 BC, the scroll was written again with “many similar words” added (Jeremiah 36:32). By the exile, the words of one prophet were being read by another as settled Scripture: Daniel “understood from the sacred books, according to the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet,” that the desolation would last seventy years (Daniel 9:2). Zechariah looks back on “the earlier prophets” as a finished witness Israel had refused (Zechariah 7:12). The written word also judged its keepers. The finding of the Book of the Law in Josiah's reign, around 622 BC (2 Kings 22:8), and Ezra's public reading after the exile, when the Levites read “explaining it and giving insight, so that the people could understand what was being read” (Nehemiah 8:8), show a people learning to live under a book. The Prophets close, in both the Hebrew and the Christian order, with Malachi pointing backward to Moses and forward to Elijah: “Remember the law of My servant Moses” (Malachi 4:4).

The shape of the Hebrew canon can be traced outside the Bible. The Greek prologue to Sirach, written by the author's grandson after he came to Egypt in about 132 BC, refers three times to ‘the Law and the Prophets and the other books’. A Qumran document known as 4QMMT speaks of the book of Moses, the books of the prophets, and David, though scholars debate how much it implies. In the 90s AD the Jewish historian Josephus, in Against Apion, said the Jews had twenty-two books of acknowledged authority, a count that most scholars match to the same contents as the twenty-four books of the later Jewish reckoning and the thirty-nine of the Protestant Old Testament, which divide the same material differently. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther is represented, alongside copies of other writings such as Tobit, Sirach, 1 Enoch, and Jubilees. Rabbinic debate over whether Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs ‘defile the hands’, the rabbinic way of marking a book as holy, is recorded in the Mishnah (Yadayim 3:5). The Greek translation begun in Alexandria in the third century BC, the Septuagint, circulated alongside other Jewish books composed or preserved in Greek, among them Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, 1 and 2 Maccabees, and additions to Esther and Daniel. These are the books Protestants call the Apocrypha and Catholics call the deuterocanonical books, ‘the second canon’. 1 Maccabees itself three times notes that no prophet was then in Israel (4:46, 9:27, 14:41), a remark that later Jewish and Protestant readers took as evidence that the prophetic writings had ceased.

The Old Testament also lays down the claims that later became the doctrine of Scripture's attributes. Its authority is God's: the Book of the Law stands beside the ark as a witness. Its necessity is plain in the famine Amos threatens, not of bread but of hearing God's word (Amos 8:11). Its sufficiency and limits are set side by side: “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us and to our children forever, so that we may follow all the words of this law” (Deuteronomy 29:29). And its clarity is celebrated: “The unfolding of Your words gives light; it informs the simple” (Psalm 119:130), and “The Law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul; the testimony of the LORD is trustworthy, making wise the simple” (Psalm 19:7).
nt:
Jesus received Israel's Scriptures as the word of God and read them as a whole that pointed to him. After the resurrection he said that “Everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms” (Luke 24:44), a threefold description that many scholars match to the shape of the Hebrew Bible, with the Psalms, the largest book of the Writings, standing for that third part. His charge that the blood of the prophets would be required “from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah” (Matthew 23:35) runs from the first murder in Genesis to the stoning of Zechariah in 2 Chronicles 24:20-21, the last book in the most common traditional Hebrew order, which many scholars read as a sign that his Bible ended where the Hebrew Bible ends (Matthew's ‘son of Berechiah’ raises an identification question that interpreters answer in different ways). Jesus argued from a single word of a psalm and said that “the Scripture cannot be broken” (John 10:35). He blamed error on ignorance of it: “You are mistaken because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God” (Matthew 22:29). And he set it above the inherited practice of his own teachers: “Thus you nullify the word of God by the tradition you have handed down” (Mark 7:13). Paul says Israel was “entrusted with the very words of God” (Romans 3:2) and that “everything that was written in the past was written for our instruction” (Romans 15:4). The New Testament writers quote or echo nearly every part of the Old Testament. Jude 14-15 quotes a prophecy of Enoch from the book now called 1 Enoch, and Hebrews 11:35 probably alludes to the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 7; interpreters differ over what these uses imply about those books' standing.

The apostles spoke and wrote with an authority they understood as Christ's own. Jesus promised that the Spirit would “remind you of everything I have told you” (John 14:26), and Paul described the church as “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone” (Ephesians 2:20). He told the Corinthians to “acknowledge that what I am writing you is the Lord’s command” (1 Corinthians 14:37), and he thanked God that the Thessalonians had received his preaching “not as the word of men, but as the true word of God” (1 Thessalonians 2:13). The letters were read aloud in the assemblies (1 Thessalonians 5:27) and passed between churches: “make sure that it is also read in the church of the Laodiceans, and that you in turn read the letter from Laodicea” (Colossians 4:16), a letter that has not survived. Forgery was already a danger, which is why Paul warned against a “letter seeming to be from us” (2 Thessalonians 2:2) and signed with his own hand (2 Thessalonians 3:17). Within the New Testament itself the new writings begin to stand beside the old. 1 Timothy 5:18 introduces two sayings with “the Scripture says”: “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain,” from Deuteronomy 25:4, and “The worker is worthy of his wages,” words found in Luke 10:7. 2 Peter 3:16 speaks of Paul's letters, which the unstable twist “as they do the rest of the Scriptures”.

The New Testament also presses the claims that became Scripture's attributes. Its sufficiency is stated in terms of purpose: the Scriptures “are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus,” and God-breathed Scripture makes the servant of God “complete, fully equipped for every good work” (2 Timothy 3:15-17). John admits that Jesus did far more than his Gospel records, “But these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name” (John 20:31). Paul teaches the Corinthians “not to go beyond what is written” (1 Corinthians 4:6), though interpreters debate exactly what writing he means. Its clarity is assumed when ordinary listeners are praised for testing an apostle by it: the Bereans “examined the Scriptures every day to see if these teachings were true” (Acts 17:11). Yet clarity never meant uniform ease, since Peter admits that “Some parts of his letters are hard to understand” (2 Peter 3:16). Its finality follows from the finality of Christ: God “has spoken to us by His Son” (Hebrews 1:2), and Jude urges the church to contend “for the faith entrusted once for all to the saints” (Jude 1:3). The warning at the close of Revelation against adding to or taking from “the words of this book of prophecy” (Revelation 22:19) guards that book in the language of Deuteronomy 4:2, and though it does not by itself define the canon, it sits fittingly at the end of it.

keyTexts.why: The first command not to add to or subtract from God's word, the root of every later concern for the canon's boundaries.
The finished Book of the Law is laid beside the ark as a witness, showing that Israel's Scripture began as a written covenant document with binding authority.
The Law is perfect, trustworthy, right, and radiant; it revives, gives wisdom to the simple, and warns. The Psalter's praise of Scripture's authority and clarity.
The prophet seals his teaching among his disciples and makes the written law and testimony the test of every rival voice.
Daniel reads Jeremiah's prophecy in ‘the sacred books’, an early sign that prophetic writings were being received as Scripture by later generations.
Jesus sets the commandment of God over the tradition of the elders, the text most often cited for Scripture's authority over later tradition.
The risen Jesus names the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms, the threefold shape of the Hebrew Bible, and opens his disciples' minds to understand them.
Jesus rests an argument on one word of Psalm 82 and says that the Scripture cannot be broken.
John states that his Gospel is selective and purposeful, written so that readers may believe and have life. Scripture is sufficient for its purpose, not exhaustive.
The church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, which is why the early church asked of every book whether it carried apostolic witness.
Paul's letters are exchanged and read aloud in the churches, the ordinary practice through which the New Testament collection took shape.
A saying of Jesus found in Luke is set beside Deuteronomy under the single heading ‘the Scripture says’.
Scripture, received from childhood, makes a person wise for salvation and fully equips for every good work, the classic text for both inspiration and sufficiency.
Paul's letters are counted with ‘the rest of the Scriptures’, and Peter admits that some of them are hard to understand, a check on any naive account of clarity.
The faith was delivered once for all to the saints, the ground for the church's conviction that the apostolic witness is complete.

history:
The early church received Israel's Scriptures, usually in Greek, together with the Gospels and apostolic letters that were read in its assemblies. The pressure to say exactly which books belonged came from rivals. In the 140s Marcion, in Rome, rejected the Old Testament and accepted only an edited Luke and ten letters of Paul. Around 180 Irenaeus of Lyon (Against Heresies 3.11.8) argued that there are four Gospels and could be no more, against gnostic teachers who produced gospels of their own. The Muratorian fragment, a Latin list usually dated to the late second century (Albert Sundberg and Geoffrey Hahneman argued for the fourth), accepts four Gospels, Acts, thirteen letters of Paul, Jude, two letters of John, and Revelation, and says the recent Shepherd of Hermas may be read but not in the church's public reading. The criteria at work were a book's link to the apostles, its agreement with the rule of faith (the summary of apostolic teaching confessed at baptism), and its long and wide use in the churches. Eusebius of Caesarea, in his Church History (3.25, early fourth century), sorted books into those acknowledged by all, those disputed (among them James, Jude, 2 Peter, and 2 and 3 John), and those spurious, and he said Revelation could be placed among the acknowledged or among the spurious, depending on the judgment of the reader. Athanasius of Alexandria's thirty-ninth Festal Letter (367) listed the twenty-seven books of the New Testament, and North African synods at Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) affirmed the same books. The Syriac churches long used a New Testament without 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude, and Revelation, and the Ethiopian church keeps a wider canon with 1 Enoch and Jubilees.

The Old Testament's edges stayed disputed longer. Melito of Sardis, around 170, recorded a list gathered in the East that matches the Hebrew books except that it lacks Esther. Athanasius counted the Hebrew books, with Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah attached to Jeremiah and without Esther, and set Wisdom, Sirach, Esther, Judith, and Tobit among books appointed to be read by new believers. Jerome, who translated the Old Testament from Hebrew for the Latin Vulgate between about 391 and 405, held that the books outside the Hebrew canon could be read for edification but not used to establish doctrine. Augustine (On Christian Doctrine 2.8) and the North African councils received them as canonical, and Pope Innocent I sent a list including them to Exsuperius of Toulouse in 405. The Council of Florence restated that wider list in 1442. The Reformation reopened the question. At the Leipzig Disputation in 1519 Luther rejected an argument drawn from 2 Maccabees, and in his New Testament of 1522 he placed Hebrews, James, Jude, and Revelation at the end, doubting their standing; his complete Bible of 1534 gathered the Apocrypha in a separate section as books not equal to Scripture but useful to read. The Council of Trent, in its fourth session on 8 April 1546, defined the canon to include the deuterocanonical books and taught that the gospel is contained in the written books and in unwritten traditions, both received with equal reverence.

The Protestant confessions set out the canon together with Scripture's attributes. The Belgic Confession (1561) listed the books, said they are received not chiefly because the church receives them but because the Holy Spirit testifies in believers' hearts that they are from God, and taught their sufficiency. The Thirty-Nine Articles of the Church of England (1563, revised 1571) said, following Jerome, that the church reads the Apocrypha for example of life and instruction in manners but does not use them to establish doctrine, and called the church a witness and keeper of Holy Writ. The Westminster Confession (1646), chapter 1, listed the sixty-six books, denied that the Apocrypha have authority beyond other human writings, grounded Scripture's authority in God its author rather than in the church, and set out its necessity, sufficiency, and clarity: the whole counsel of God is either expressly set down in Scripture or can be deduced from it by good and necessary consequence, and what is needed for salvation is clear enough that the unlearned can understand it by ordinary means. Luther's The Bondage of the Will (1525) defended Scripture's clarity against Erasmus, and Calvin (Institutes 1.7) taught that Scripture is self-authenticating, confirmed to believers by the inward testimony of the Spirit. The Eastern churches answered the Reformation at the Synod of Jerusalem (1672), whose Confession of Dositheus called Wisdom, Judith, Tobit, the Maccabees, Sirach, and the Greek additions to Daniel genuine parts of Scripture.

Modern debate has come from several directions. The First Vatican Council (Dei Filius, 1870) taught that the church holds the books as sacred not because it approved them but because they were written by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit and have God as their author. Because Trent's final decree had replaced a draft wording (that the gospel is found ‘partly’ in Scripture and ‘partly’ in tradition) with a simple ‘and’, Josef Rupert Geiselmann argued in the 1950s that Catholic teaching allows all saving truth to be found in Scripture, and the Second Vatican Council's Dei Verbum (1965) described Scripture and Tradition as flowing from one divine wellspring and the teaching office as the servant, not the master, of the word of God. Critical historians since Walter Bauer (1934) have presented the canon as the outcome of contested church history, while Bruce Metzger's The Canon of the New Testament (1987) traced how its core was recognized early and widely. Brevard Childs's Introduction to the Old Testament as Scripture (1979) turned attention to the books' final canonical shape. The site's systematic pages survey these views at length at /theology/doctrine/scripture, /theology/doctrine/ot-canon, /theology/doctrine/nt-canon, and /theology/doctrine/apocrypha.

differ.view: Protestant: a self-authenticating canon of sixty-six books
differ.body: Protestant churches hold that the canon is not created by the church but recognized by it, as sheep recognize their shepherd's voice. The Old Testament is the Hebrew Bible entrusted to Israel, which Jesus and the apostles received; the books outside it were valued but never cited by the New Testament as Scripture with the formula ‘it is written’, and Jerome, the church's great Hebraist, set them apart. The New Testament is the apostolic witness, recognized by the churches over the first centuries. Because Scripture is God's word, it stands above every later tradition as the only infallible rule, while creeds and the church's teaching are valued as faithful but fallible servants of the text. The Spirit's inward testimony, not a council's decree, is the final ground of the believer's confidence.

differ.view: Roman Catholic: the canon of seventy-three books, known through the church
differ.body: Catholic teaching holds that the same Spirit who inspired the books guided the church to recognize them, and that the church's discernment is the means by which Christians know with certainty which books are inspired. The early church read the Old Testament largely in its Greek form, and the councils of Hippo and Carthage, with Augustine, received the deuterocanonical books; Innocent I, Florence, and finally Trent confirmed that list. Scripture and Tradition are not rival sources but flow from one wellspring, the apostolic deposit, and the teaching office serves the word by interpreting it faithfully. On this view, the Protestant appeal to Scripture alone already relies on a table of contents the church supplied.

differ.view: Eastern Orthodox: Scripture within Holy Tradition
differ.body: Orthodox churches understand Scripture as the heart of Holy Tradition, the church's living memory of the apostolic faith, rather than as a separate authority set over against it. Their Old Testament follows the Septuagint and includes books beyond the Catholic list, such as 1 Esdras, 3 Maccabees, the Prayer of Manasseh, and Psalm 151, often described as anagignoskomena, ‘books to be read’. The canon's edges have been defined less sharply than in the West, because the question is settled in practice by what the church reads in its worship. The Synod of Jerusalem (1672) affirmed the wider books against those who called them apocrypha. Georges Florovsky's essays on Bible, church, and tradition are a standard modern statement of this view.

differ.view: Lutheran and Anglican: the Apocrypha read, but not for doctrine
differ.body: The Lutheran and Anglican churches kept the Apocrypha in their Bibles and read portions of them in public worship, while denying them authority to establish doctrine. Luther's 1534 Bible and the Thirty-Nine Articles both follow Jerome's line. Defenders of this path argue that it honors the ancient church's reading habits and the real value of books such as Sirach and Wisdom, while keeping the Hebrew canon as the measure of doctrine. It also leaves room for the historic distinction, found in Eusebius and in Luther, between books whose apostolic standing was never doubted and those that were long disputed, without removing any of the twenty-seven New Testament books.

errors:
The church rejected Marcion's attempt, in the second century, to cut away the Old Testament and trim the New to fit his theology; the Old Testament is the Scripture Jesus read, and the God of Israel is the Father of Jesus Christ. It rejected the gnostic claim to secret gospels and hidden traditions available only to the initiated, answering that the apostolic faith was public and handed down openly in the churches. The popular modern story that the canon was voted into being at the Council of Nicaea in 325, repeated in Dan Brown's novel The Da Vinci Code (2003), has no basis: Nicaea dealt with the deity of Christ, the date of Easter, and church order, and the recognition of the books was a long process in the churches before and after it. Christians of every tradition also reject the claim of later movements to add new books to the completed apostolic witness, as when the Latter-day Saints receive the Book of Mormon (1830) as Scripture.

Within the church, two opposite distortions recur. One treats the Bible as a detached oracle to be read by each person alone, with no creed, community, or history of reading, a stance sometimes called ‘solo scriptura’ to distinguish it from the Reformers' sola scriptura, which read Scripture as its final authority but within the church and with the creeds. The other buries Scripture under tradition, custom, or the latest private revelation, so that the word of God is nullified by what is handed down, the very fault Jesus named in Mark 7. A third mistake confuses clarity with ease, as though every passage were equally plain, or confuses sufficiency with exhaustiveness, as though the Bible were meant to answer every question of science, medicine, or politics rather than to make a person wise for salvation and equipped for every good work.
life:
To receive a canon is to agree that God has spoken and that what he said can be read. That frees a Christian from two anxieties: the fear that faith rests on nothing but feeling, and the pressure to invent a message for oneself. The Bible is sufficient, which means a believer need not hunt for secret knowledge or extraordinary experiences to find God's will for salvation and holiness; it is clear, which means an ordinary person with an ordinary translation, prayer, and the help of the church can understand what matters most. It is also a discipline. The canon was given as a whole, so reading only favorite books shrinks the God one knows, and the long history of how the church received these books is a reminder that no reader is the first to open them.

The doctrine shapes prayer and hope as well. Christians pray the Psalms because they are Scripture, and they bring Scripture's promises back to God in their own requests. A closed canon means that God's word is not waiting to be revised by the next generation, and that the promises made to Abraham, spoken by the prophets, and fulfilled in Christ still stand for anyone who reads them. Isaiah's confidence belongs to every reader of the whole Bible: “The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever” (Isaiah 40:8).
questions: Jesus described his Bible as the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms. What does it change to read the Old Testament as the Scripture Jesus himself read and prayed?
The early church asked whether a book was apostolic, agreed with the rule of faith, and was widely used. Which of these tests seems most important to you, and why?
Where are you most tempted either to add to Scripture (with tradition, experience, or preference) or to take from it (by ignoring the parts you find hard)?
